newsitem.title: MONACO: OLYMPICS-NO BOXING JUDGES CHEATED AT 1988 GAMES, SAY IOC.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-NO BOXING JUDGES CHEATED AT 1988 GAMES, SAY IOC.

text.p: Olympic chiefs said on Tuesday they had found no evidence to support allegations of corruption in the boxing events at the 1988 Seoul Games.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) said it had found no proof to support accusations that American light-middleweight Roy Jones was cheated out of a gold medal by dishonest judges and would not be taking any action in the case.
"There is no evidence of corruption in the boxing events in Seoul," IOC director general Francois Carrard said at the end of an investigation into the much-publicised scandal.
Jones, who went on to become a professional world champion, was beaten in the 1988 final by South Korean Park Si-hun after an extraordinary decision.
Most spectators and commentators present had Jones way ahead of his outclassed opponent but three judges from Morocco, Uruguay and Uganda gave the decision to Park.
Last year the IOC appointed a commission to investigate allegations that some judges were bribed in favour of South Koreans and that some international boxing officials were aware of the cheating.
But the IOC said in a statement: "The facts obtained by the working group have not added any new elements that would warrant reviewing the decision taken by the judges."
Carrard said he had travelled to Morocco in March to discuss the affair with the Moroccan judge in the Jones fight, Hiouad Larbi, who denies taking bribes. The IOC also studied videos of the bout.

"Larbi made an excellent impression," Carrard said. "He said that if he had to judge it today, he would judge it in exactly the same way although he acknowledged that some people might see it another way."

In a transcript of the interview made available by the IOC, Larbi said he had received $300 from the Seoul organisers to cover the cost of food in Korea which was high by African standards. This payment was made to all the African judges, he said.
"This indemnity was given to us without any condition or consideration whatsoever," he said. "I am categorical about this...

"I very much hope that this interview will clear once and for all the suspicions which have unjustly rested upon me. I consider myself always to have been an impartial, honest and fair judge and referee in all circumstances."

Some of the evidence for the accusations was contained in files provided by former East Germany's state security police -- the Stasi -- which took a great interest in sport and had compiled reports on the Seoul boxing after a briefing from an international amateur boxing chief.
But Carrard said Stasi files were not always accurate because facts were often not checked.
